name: hylomorphism
intent: Compose an unfold with a fold over one shared shape so that a seed is expanded and immediately collapsed by a single recursion, eliminating the intermediate structure that a separate unfold and fold would allocate.
problem: An unfold produces a structure (a list, a tree, a parse shape) and the very next step folds that structure away into a result, so the structure is pure overhead: it is allocated, traversed twice, and never observed. You must decide whether to keep the two recursions separate - materialize, then consume - or fuse them into one recursion that never builds the middle: unfold then fold, one recursion, no intermediate structure.
context: Applies wherever a producer and a consumer form a pipeline over the same shape: parsing then evaluating, partitioning then recombining (quicksort, mergesort, FFT), difference and metric algorithms (edit distance), compiler passes, and streaming aggregations. In a lazy language the two-phase program may already fuse by deforestation, so the hylomorphism is often just the way you write the fusion down; in strict languages the fusion must be built deliberately - a single-pass loop, or the language's lazy iteration protocol (generators, iterators, streams) - or the intermediate structure really is allocated.
benefits: The intermediate structure is never allocated, so the computation runs in the space its fold actually needs - often constant instead of O(size); this is the deforestation effect of fusing the two recursions.
One traversal instead of two: each layer is produced and consumed in the same step, cutting allocation, cache traffic and GC pressure.

When the fold is lazy or the loop is eager, results can be consumed incrementally and the consumer can stop early, whereas two-phase code must finish the entire unfold before the first result is produced.
The producer and the consumer stay independently reusable and testable: the coalgebra composes with other algebras, the algebra with other coalgebras, and the recursion scheme owns the control flow.
The intermediate type can disappear from the API: only the seed and result types stay public, so callers cannot come to depend on a transient tree that is an implementation detail.
tradeoffs: Fusion converts heap into stack: the eliminated structure is replaced by call depth, so a deeply nested or unbounded unfold can overflow the stack where the materialized version would not.
No natural early exit: a plain hylomorphism has no escape hatch, and short-circuiting requires an Elgot-style Either in the coalgebra or exceptions, both of which contaminate the pure shape.
The intermediate structure becomes invisible, removing the artifact you would otherwise inspect, log or assert on; debugging drops to reasoning about an abstract recursion.

Fusing forfeits memoization and sharing: if the structure feeds several consumers, a cache or a second traversal, recomputation - or an ad-hoc reintroduced buffer - replaces the sharing the two-phase form gave for free.
Both halves must be shaped by the same base functor, so a change to the produced shape ripples into the consumer and the apparently independent algebra and coalgebra must co-evolve.
It adds a vocabulary (coalgebra, algebra, hylo) to code whose lazy pipeline already is the fused form; in a Rust iterator chain or a LINQ query the abstraction can read as ceremony.

In strict languages the fused code is not automatically tail-recursive: deforestation eliminates the intermediate structure but leaves a non-tail recursive loop, so explicit accumulator threading is needed for constant space.

participants.responsibility: The initial state the unfold starts from; carried through each step and, in the fused form, never materialized as any other value.
Given one state, produce one layer of the structure plus its successor states, or signal termination (None/Empty/Nil).
Combine one already-folded layer into a result; its carrier type is the hylomorphism's result type.
The pattern functor both halves share (list, tree, rose, expression); the composition is only defined where both sides use the same shape.
The single recursion that calls the coalgebra, recurses on the successors and applies the algebra on the way back - hylo alg coalg = cata alg . ana coalg - owning termination and stack behaviour.

use_cases: Parse and evaluate in one pass: a token stream or S-expression is unfolded from the input and immediately folded into a value, so no parse tree exists at runtime (the RPN calculator of the recursion-schemes literature).
Divide and conquer: quicksort, mergesort and the FFT expressed as partition-unfold plus combine-fold, with the recursion tree fused away by construction.
Difference and metric algorithms: edit distance, Levenshtein and similar dynamic-programming recurrences written as an unfold of the option tree plus a min/plus fold over it.
Streaming aggregation: a generator over a file, page or sensor feed drives an accumulator in the same pass, so no batch of records is ever materialized.
Compiler and interpreter passes: build an intermediate representation from a seed and lower it to the target immediately, never holding both representations at once.
Large tree, JSON or XML transformations where only the folded result is needed and the document must not be held twice in memory.

Memoized dynamic programming: combining histomorphism (course-of-value recursion with full subterm history) with unfold/fold to express knapsack, CYK parsing, and similar tabulation problems without a hand-written table.

Report generation from hierarchical data: unfold a configuration or schema into a structured template and fold it into a formatted document (PDF sections, HTML output, CSV rows), materializing only the final byte stream.
Adversarial search: game tree evaluation (minimax, alpha-beta pruning) expressed as unfold of game states and fold of scores, where only the best path score is kept at any depth.

Program synthesis with genetic programming: the Origami algorithm uses hylomorphism templates to constrain the search space — the synthesizer fills in the algebra and coalgebra gaps, dramatically reducing the candidate program space (GPSB benchmark suite, arXiv 2024).

Hardware kernel extraction: divide-and-conquer algorithms expressed as hylomorphisms enable automatic extraction and optimisation of hardware kernels, where the intermediate structure is never materialized in the circuit.

Higher-order recursion scheme (HORS) model checking: temporal properties of programs are verified by encoding the program as a hylomorphism-derived tree and model-checking the resulting tree against a temporal logic specification.

Streaming/coinductive pipelines: when the producer generates at a different rate than the consumer, a chronomorphism (a temporal generalisation of hylomorphism) models the time-varying interaction; the plain hylomorphism applies when rates are matched and exact fusion is possible.

Scala fixed-point libraries in compiler-shaped code: Droste (higherkindness/droste) exposes ghylo/hylo over Cats and ships athema, a math-expression parser, as its worked hylomorphism example; Matryoshka (precog/matryoshka) exposes hyloF/hyloM and points to the 'Efficient Nanopass Compilers using Cats and Matryoshka' line of work applying these schemes to compiler passes.

Automated deforestation tooling: the DrHylo tool implements the Hu-Iwasaki-Takeichi ICFP'96 algorithm that mechanically rewrites ordinary recursive definitions into structural hylomorphisms precisely because hylo-shaped recursions fuse, so the intermediate structure is removed by construction rather than by hand.

Graph-closure pipelines in pure Nix: Nix-ecosystem libraries such as sini/gen-graph traverse graphs with a hylomorphism-like shape - a visited-set coalgebra unfolds a possibly cyclic graph into a finite DFS forest while a fold assembles the accumulator in the same traversal, never materializing the forest.
avoid_when: The structure is needed more than once (re-traversal, memoization, sharing, a second consumer): build it once and fold it many times - that is Fold/Catamorphism plus Unfold/Anamorphism, not a hylomorphism.
The unfold must stop early on a condition discovered while folding and the language offers no cheap escape: the two-phase version can simply stop, the plain hylomorphism cannot.
The generated sequence is itself the deliverable API (a lazy list, an iterator, a stream): expose the producer and let callers fold it, rather than hiding the reusable artifact inside one consumer.
The structure is small or the pass is cold: the abstraction and the fused code cost more to read than a straightforward two-step version costs to run.
You need the intermediate representation for logs, tests, audit or debugging, where an invisible structure is a liability rather than a saving.
anti_patterns: Naming it fusion while still materializing: unfold into a list and then reduce over that list, annotated as a hylomorphism - the allocation the pattern removes is still there.
Forcing unlike shapes together: a coalgebra whose shape differs from the algebra's, bridged with a queue or a channel, which recreates the intermediate structure under another name.
Wrapping an existing lazy pipeline in hand-rolled hylo machinery (a Rust iterator chain, a LINQ query, a Java stream) and obscuring the idiom the language already documents.
Deepening recursion without regard for the stack: replacing a heap structure with unbounded call depth and treating the resulting overflow as a language problem.
Short-circuiting by throwing exceptions out of a fused recursion instead of choosing an Elgot-style escalation or the two-phase form.
Using a recursive functor (e.g., []) as the base functor and causing non-termination instead of a non-recursive base functor (e.g., ListF) with a fixed-point wrapper.
Forgetting to INLINE the generic catamorphism wrapper in GHC, so fmap layers are not fused and deforestation fails silently.
design_principles: Deforestation/fusion: two recursions over a transient structure can be composed into one recursion that never builds it.
Separation of concerns: what to generate (coalgebra) is stated apart from how to combine (algebra), while the recursion scheme owns the control flow.
Composition over materialization: producers and consumers compose instead of storing intermediate values.
Well-foundedness: the recursion terminates because every coalgebra step descends, so termination is a property of the descent rather than of a fuel counter.
Parametricity over the shape (base functor): one driver serves list, tree and expression shapes, so the recursion logic is written once.
Accumulator discipline in strict languages: fusion eliminates intermediate heap allocation but not stack depth; the algebra must thread an accumulator for constant space.
best_practices: Write the algebra and the coalgebra as separate, individually testable functions and keep the fused driver a one-liner or a small loop.
Fix the base functor both halves share and keep the seed type explicit, so the driver's signature (Alg -> Coalg -> seed -> result) documents the pattern at the call site.

In strict languages express the fusion through the language's lazy mechanism (generator, iterator, sequence) so producer and consumer interleave; reserve the hand-written loop for hot arithmetic paths.
Measure before fusing: when the structure is reused or the pass is cold, the materialized version is clearer and sometimes faster.
Watch the stack: prefer a lazy iterator over deep recursion when the unfold is deeply nested or unbounded, and test with adversarial depth.
When early termination is required, use an Either/Elgot-style exit in the coalgebra instead of exceptions, and document where the escape happens.
In GHC Haskell, always mark the catamorphism wrapper INLINE so GHC can see through it and fuse the fmap layers; without this the generic implementation defeats deforestation.
For constant-space results in strict languages, pass an accumulator through the algebra explicitly; do not rely on the fused code being tail-recursive automatically.
Use a non-recursive base functor (e.g., ListF a l = Nil | Cons a l) rather than a recursive functor (e.g., []) as the shape, to guarantee termination on corner cases.
When multiple consumers need the structure, prefer Fold + Unfold with explicit sharing over a single hylomorphism that hides the materialization.
In Scala use Matryoshka's hyloF for pure hylomorphisms and hyloM for monadic effect chains (e.g., database or IO in the coalgebra or algebra).
In Rust use ordofp::recursion::hylo or karpal-recursion; prefer hylo over separate ana + cata when the structure has a single consumer and allocation matters.
Validate the base functor match between algebra and coalgebra with a unit test that asserts the intermediate type never appears in the public API surface.

Test the algebra and coalgebra independently before testing the composed hylomorphism: write unit tests for each function in isolation and property-based tests for the functorlaws (identity, composition) on the base functor — errors in the base functor are the most subtle to debug once fused.

In lazy languages, watch for thunk space leaks: the fused form can retain references to parts of the seed that the materialised form would release earlier; use seq or bang patterns to force cleanup points when strictness is needed.

When debugging a fused hylomorphism, temporarily separate the unfold from the fold to recover the intermediate structure for inspection; annotate the boundary with a newtype wrapper to surface where the structure should appear.

For stream processing with back-pressure, prefer a chronomorphism (chronologism) over a plain hylomorphism: it models producer-consumer rate differences explicitly and makes time-bounded buffering visible in the type.

In a strict language, always write a strict accumulator version alongside the lazy one when constant space is required: the fused hylo is not automatically tail-recursive and the extra stack depth can cause crashes on deep inputs.

Use the type-signature heuristic from the Origami program synthesis literature (arXiv 2024) to choose between catamorphism, anamorphism, and hylomorphism: a type a -> b suggests hylomorphism, f a -> b suggests catamorphism, a -> f b suggests anamorphism.

Property-based testing of the hylomorphism invariant: given the same seed, hylo(alg, coalg, seed) must equal fold(alg, unfold(coalg, seed)) for all seeds; a shrinking property test makes this a strong regression suite.
